The domains: air, water, food, soil, climate, built environment — one line and one original example each

claims.claim: WHO's published framing of environmental health: good health depends on clean air, a stable climate, a preserved natural environment, and access to adequate water, sanitation and hygiene, and requires protection from harmful radiation, unsafe chemical management, and unhealthy working conditions; WHO/Europe describes the field's purpose as protecting human health from the risks of a hazardous or contaminated environment through primary prevention and intersectoral collaboration.

The environment affects health: if parts of the environment like the air, water, or soil become polluted, it can lead to health problems; some environmental risks are natural (radon in soil), while others result from human activities (lead poisoning from paint, asbestos or mercury from mining or industrial use).
In 2016, 13.7 million deaths — 24% of global fatalities — were attributed to modifiable environmental risks, meaning nearly one in four global deaths is linked to environmental conditions.

Exposure is contact between people and hazards: the CDC Principles of Epidemiology glossary defines exposure as contact with a disease-causing factor or the amount of the factor that makes contact with a population; the lesson states the idea simply as contact between people and hazards (breathing, drinking, touching).

Environmental hazards are commonly grouped into three broad types — chemical (lead, pesticides, mercury), physical (radiation, noise, extreme heat), and biological (bacteria, viruses, parasites, mold) — a classification synthesized from MedlinePlus's pollution examples, WHO's radiation/chemical-management framing, and WHO's food-safety description of bacteria, viruses, parasites, and chemical substances in food.

Some groups face higher exposures: infants, young children, older people, and people who are ill are especially affected by contaminated food, and WHO describes the health impacts of poor environmental conditions as running through social inequalities as well as direct contact.

The field's work includes monitoring, regulation, cleanup, and research: WHO describes the work as monitoring health risks, assessing whether implemented solutions are effective, steering research, sharing evidence-based knowledge, and supporting governance, norms, and policies that reduce environmental risks; in the United States, the EPA's Superfund program protects human health by cleaning up contaminated sites and making responsible parties pay for cleanup.

Built environments are part of environmental health: WHO lists health-supportive cities and built environments among the prerequisites for good health (2021 capture of the WHO environmental health health-topic page).

Unsafe food contaminated with bacteria, viruses, parasites, or chemical substances can cause more than 200 different diseases, ranging from diarrhea to cancers; food safety is therefore a core environmental health domain.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact WHO working-definition sentence ('Environmental health addresses all the physical, chemical, and biological factors external to a person...') is widely quoted in secondary literature, but the exact string could not be verified on any current or archived WHO page during this research session.
positions: Quote the classic sentence and attribute it to WHO as a verbatim definition (common in textbooks).

Attribute only what is verifiable on WHO pages: the health-topic overview ('Good health depends on clean air, a stable climate, a preserved natural environment, as well as access to adequate water, sanitation and hygiene...') and WHO/Europe's description of protecting health from hazardous or contaminated environments.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the verifiable option: it presents a working description attributed to WHO as a paraphrase of WHO's published overview and WHO/Europe's field description, and never prints the unverified sentence as a quotation. The evidence packet notes the discrepancy so a future session can upgrade to the exact quote if a canonical WHO page is located.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's definition of environmental health as 'a foundational Public Health concept' with no field-specific content — replaced with an attributed working description.
The draft's generic framing that environmental health is 'most useful when you can define it, recognize where it applies, and explain its limits' — discarded as non-substantive boilerplate.
The draft's worked example ('A student reads a short Public Health scenario...') — replaced with a concrete original scenario.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate draft with a source-verified lesson: working description attributed to WHO's published overview and WHO/Europe's field description (paraphrase, not an unverified verbatim quote).
Added the verified disease-burden figure: 13.7 million deaths in 2016, 24% of global deaths, attributed to modifiable environmental risks (WHO).

Added source-backed exposure, hazard-type, domain, and vulnerable-population claims; reused existing registry records cdc-principles-of-epidemiology-glossary and who-food-safety with identical ids and URLs.

rightsIssues: All sources used reference-only or public-domain: no source prose reproduced; WHO, MedlinePlus/NIH, EPA, and CDC facts are synthesized in original wording. The MedlinePlus page is NIH-produced; EPA and CDC pages are U.S. government works (public domain).

sourceRecords.title: What is Superfund?
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22. Supports the cleanup function: Superfund's goals are to protect human health and the environment by cleaning up contaminated sites, make responsible parties pay for cleanup work, involve communities in the Superfund process, and return Superfund sites to productive use. U.S. government work; facts synthesized, no wording reproduced.
